text: Everyone in the village knew that Helen Turrell, a respectable woman of good family, had always done her duty by everyone, and above all by her only brothers unfortunate child. <break time="0.8s" /> George, who served as a police inspector in India, had become entangled with the daughter of a retired sergeant, and then he was killed by a fall from his horse. <break time="0.8s" /> His death came only a few weeks before his son was born, and Helen, then resting in the south of France for her weak lungs, resolved to take charge of the child. <break time="0.8s" /> Helen arranged for the baby to be brought from Bombay to Marseilles, where she met him and took him into her own care at once. <break time="0.8s" /> Soon the baby fell ill with dysentery because of a careless nurse, whom Helen promptly dismissed before nursing the child back to health herself. <break time="0.8s" /> Late that autumn she came home to Hampshire with the boy, whom she had already had christened Michael, and settled down to raise him in her own house. <break time="0.8s" /> Helen never tried to hide the facts, for she believed that scandals only grow larger when they are hushed up, and so she spoke of them freely to anyone who asked. <break time="0.8s" /> As she told it, Michael was simply her dead brothers son, and she had agreed, out of duty and affection, to bring him up as her nephew.
